questions.question:
D1 — Add gstack skill routing rules to CLAUDE.md?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-X1N3st on main, reviewing PLAN.md (Multi-tenant Auth Refactor).
ELI10: gstack works best when your project's CLAUDE.md includes skill routing rules, so that saying "review the architecture" or "ship it" automatically invokes the right skill. This is a one-time setup prompt per project. Plan mode is active, so the CLAUDE.md edit and commit would happen after this review exits plan mode.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Without routing, you invoke skills by name manually; with it, an unwanted auto-invoke could surprise you.
Recommendation: A because routing removes friction and is trivially reversible (delete the section).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: convenience of auto-routing vs. keeping CLAUDE.md minimal.

options.label: A) Add routing rules (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Natural-language requests route to the right gstack skill without remembering names. ✅ One-time append, reversible by deleting the section. ❌ Adds a block to CLAUDE.md and one commit; deferred until plan mode exits.

options.label: B) No thanks, invoke manually
options.description: ✅ CLAUDE.md stays exactly as it is, no extra commit on this fixture repo. ✅ You keep full control over when a skill runs. ❌ You must type /skill-name each time; records routing_declined so this is not re-asked.

questions.question:
D2 — Run /office-hours first, or proceed with the standard eng review?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-X1N3st on main, PLAN.md has no design doc behind it.
ELI10: No design doc found for this branch. /office-hours produces a structured problem statement, premise challenge, and explored alternatives, which gives this review sharper input (about 10 minutes). The design doc is per-feature, not per-product. Without it, I review the plan as written and infer the problem statement from it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Skipping means the review may lock in an approach whose premise was never challenged; running it costs ten minutes before any architecture findings land.
Recommendation: B because the plan already states its architecture and the user request asks for the reviewed plan directly; premise questions surface in Step 0 anyway.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: sharper upstream input vs. getting to the architecture findings now.

options.label: B) Skip — standard review (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Review starts immediately against PLAN.md as written, matching the stated request. ✅ Step 0 scope challenge still questions the premise (4 new classes, 12 files). ❌ No formal alternatives-explored record; premise challenge is lighter.

options.label: A) Run /office-hours now
options.description: ✅ Produces a design doc with problem statement and alternatives (human: ~1h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ Review then has a source of truth for constraints and chosen approach. ❌ Delays architecture findings and adds a doc to maintain for a refactor whose direction is already chosen.

questions.question:
D3 — Enable cross-project learnings search?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-X1N3st on main; first time this setting is checked on this machine.
ELI10: gstack can search learnings from your other projects on this machine to find patterns that might apply here. This stays local, no data leaves your machine. Recommended for solo developers. Skip if you work on multiple client codebases where cross-contamination would be a concern.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Enabling on a multi-client machine could surface one client's patterns while reviewing another's; disabling loses reusable pitfalls you already learned elsewhere.
Recommendation: A because learnings compound and the search is local-only and reversible via gstack-config.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: compounding knowledge across repos vs. strict per-project isolation.

options.label: A) Enable cross-project (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Past pitfalls and patterns from other repos inform this review automatically. ✅ Local only; one config flag, reversible any time. ❌ On a machine shared across client codebases, unrelated patterns could bleed into findings.

options.label: B) Keep project-scoped only
options.description: ✅ Strict isolation; nothing from other repos appears in this review. ✅ Safest choice for consultants working across clients. ❌ Zero learnings exist for this project yet, so the search returns nothing this session.

questions.question:
D4 — Scope: reduce the 5 new types to 2, or proceed as planned?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (PLAN.md:19-20, 34-36).
ELI10: The plan adds AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache, TokenStore and RequestPolicy across 12 files. But AuthCache is described as a facade over the existing cache adapter with one backing cache (PLAN.md:11-13), which means it is a wrapper that adds no rules of its own. TokenStore and RequestPolicy are named once and never given a job. That is three cache-shaped things (adapter, AuthCache, TokenStore) where one exists and works, plus a policy class with no stated behavior. Every extra type is a place a 3am bug can hide and a file a new engineer has to learn.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Too much scope means a 12-file auth diff nobody can review in one sitting; too little means we cut a type that had a real purpose the plan just failed to write down.
Recommendation: A because the existing adapter already carries the tenant-key and invalidation rules, so injecting it directly into the two real services keeps every behavior and deletes two wrappers and one mystery class. Maps to your preference for engineered-enough and right-sized diff.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: two services with an injected, already-tested dependency vs. five types and a global singleton for the same behavior.

options.label: A) Reduce to AuthBroker + SessionMint (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Both services take the existing cache adapter via constructor injection; AuthCache facade and TokenStore are dropped, RequestPolicy becomes a plain typed config object plus one pure function (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min). ✅ Roughly 7-8 files instead of 12, and the adapter's existing tests keep covering the cache contract. ❌ If TokenStore or RequestPolicy had a real distinct responsibility, the plan must be amended to state it before this reduction holds.

options.label: B) Proceed as-is with all 5 types
options.description: ✅ No re-planning; implementation starts from the current document (human: ~1 week / CC: ~1.5 h). ✅ Each concept gets its own named home, which some teams prefer for future growth. ❌ 12-file auth diff with a global mutable singleton and two undocumented classes; review sections will still flag the singleton separately.

options.label: C) Middle: keep AuthCache as the one injected boundary, drop TokenStore
options.description: ✅ AuthCache stays as a named service-facing type but is passed in, not exported as a global; TokenStore is removed; RequestPolicy kept as a class (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min). ✅ Preserves a seam for future cache-policy changes without the singleton. ❌ Still a facade with no rules of its own over one backing cache, and RequestPolicy remains undefined.

questions.question:
D5 — Issue 1 [P1] (confidence 8/10) PLAN.md:10,19-20: who owns writes to the shared cache?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Architecture section.
ELI10: The plan says both AuthBroker and SessionMint mutate the same cache and that the cache rules "do not serialize mutations" (PLAN.md:10). Picture this: a tenant is suspended, the adapter's hook invalidates every entry for that tenant, and a millisecond later SessionMint finishes minting a session it started before the suspension and writes it back. The suspended tenant now has a live cached session until it expires. Same story for logout and token revocation. Injection (D4) fixes the global-variable smell but not this race; two writers with no ordering rule is still two writers.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A revoked or suspended tenant keeps working against your system for up to a token lifetime, silently, with nothing in the logs.
Recommendation: 1A because a single writer plus an epoch check is explicit, easy to test, and the adapter already has the invalidation hooks to bump the epoch. Maps to your explicit-over-clever preference.
Completeness: 1A=10/10, 1B=7/10, 1C=3/10
Net: an ordering rule that costs one integer compare vs. a race that only shows up in production.

options.label: 1A) Single writer + invalidation epoch (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Only AuthBroker writes to the adapter; SessionMint returns minted material to the broker, which stores it (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min). ✅ Adapter keeps a per-tenant invalidation epoch, bumped by the existing logout/revoke/suspend hooks; a write whose captured epoch is stale is dropped and logged. Test: suspend-during-mint asserts no entry lands. ❌ SessionMint gains a return value and the adapter gains one epoch counter per tenant; slightly larger diff.

options.label: 1B) Both write, but every write checks the epoch
options.description: ✅ No ownership change; each service reads the tenant epoch before its work and passes it on write (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min). ✅ Still closes the suspend-during-mint window with the same drop-and-log rule. ❌ Two writers means two places to forget the epoch check; the invariant lives in convention, not structure.

options.label: 1C) Accept the race, document it
options.description: ✅ Zero code; plan gains a paragraph naming the window and its bound (token TTL) (human: ~10 min / CC: ~2 min). ✅ Fine if token TTLs are seconds and suspension is rare. ❌ Suspended tenants stay live for a full TTL; no test can prove the window is as small as you think.

questions.question:
D6 — Issue 2 [P1] (confidence 8/10) PLAN.md:27-28: how does the new flow replace legacyAuthFlow()?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Architecture section.
ELI10: The plan says legacyAuthFlow() "will get rewritten as part of this work" and nothing more. That is a big-bang swap of the login path for every tenant at once. If the new AuthBroker path has a bug that only one tenant's IDP configuration triggers, every tenant is down until you revert the whole deploy. The alternative is a strangler fig: keep legacyAuthFlow() intact, put a per-tenant switch in front, route a canary tenant to AuthBroker, widen, then delete the legacy function in a follow-up PR once it takes zero traffic.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Auth is the front door. A bad big-bang means every user of every tenant sees login failures at the same moment, and rollback means redeploying.
Recommendation: 2A because a per-tenant flag makes the cost of being wrong one tenant for one minute, and the legacy path stays as the oracle for the regression tests Section 3 will require. Maps to your right-sized-diff preference: this is a necessary two-step, not a compressed rewrite.
Completeness: 2A=10/10, 2B=7/10, 2C=3/10
Net: two small PRs with a kill switch vs. one large PR with a redeploy as the only undo.

options.label: 2A) Per-tenant flag, strangler fig, delete later (recommended)
options.description: ✅ A routing function reads a per-tenant flag (default: legacy) and dispatches to legacyAuthFlow() or AuthBroker; both paths log the same structured outcome so they can be compared (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min). ✅ Rollback is a flag flip, not a deploy; legacy stays as the regression oracle; deletion is a separate trivial PR. ❌ Two code paths coexist for the rollout window; the flag plumbing is a small amount of code that gets deleted later.

options.label: 2B) Global flag, all tenants at once, flip in prod
options.description: ✅ One boolean, no per-tenant plumbing; still reversible without a deploy (human: ~2 h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ Legacy path stays available as the oracle during the window. ❌ No canary: the first flip exposes every tenant simultaneously, so a tenant-specific IDP quirk hits everyone.

options.label: 2C) Rewrite in place as planned
options.description: ✅ Smallest final codebase immediately; no flag to clean up (human: ~0 extra / CC: ~0 extra). ✅ No dual-path period to reason about. ❌ Rollback is a redeploy; no live oracle for behavior comparison; a single bug takes down login for all tenants.

answers.D6 \u2014 Issue 2 [P1] (confidence 8/10): 2A) Per-tenant flag, strangler fig, delete later (recommended)

questions.question:
D7 — Issue 3 [P1] (confidence 9/10) PLAN.md:23-24: validateAndDispatch() swallows three error classes in nested try/catch.
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Code Quality section.
ELI10: The plan describes a 60-line function with three nested try/catch blocks where "each catch swallows a different error class." Swallowing means the error is caught and the function keeps going as if nothing happened. In an auth path that is the worst possible default: a signature-verification error that gets swallowed becomes a request that proceeds. Nested try/catch also hides which stage failed, so the on-call engineer at 3am sees "dispatch failed" with no cause. The plan does not say whether this function is being touched, but the refactor routes through it, so it is in scope.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Silent auth failures that look like success, and error logs that cannot tell you which of three stages broke.
Recommendation: 3A because splitting into one function per stage with a single typed error boundary is explicit, removes the nesting, and makes each catch a tested branch. Maps to your explicit-over-clever and DRY preferences: one error mapper instead of three ad hoc catches.
Completeness: 3A=10/10, 3B=6/10, 3C=2/10
Net: three small pure functions and one error mapper vs. a 60-line function whose failure modes are invisible.

options.label: 3A) Split per stage, one typed error boundary, fail closed (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Extract validateToken(), resolvePolicy(), dispatch() as pure-ish stage functions; a single outer boundary maps each error class to a typed AuthError with a stage tag, logs it with tenant and stage, and fails closed (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min). ✅ Every former swallow becomes an explicit branch with its own unit test; the stage tag makes 3am triage a one-line grep. ❌ Behavior change: callers that relied on a swallowed error proceeding will now get a rejection, so the characterization tests in Section 3 must pin the current behavior first.

options.label: 3B) Keep the shape, stop swallowing
options.description: ✅ Minimal edit: each catch logs and rethrows a typed error instead of returning silently (human: ~2 h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ Closes the silent-success hole without restructuring. ❌ Nesting and the 60-line body remain; stage attribution still depends on reading the stack trace.

options.label: 3C) Leave it alone this PR
options.description: ✅ Zero risk of changing behavior callers depend on; smallest diff (human: 0 / CC: 0). ✅ Can be revisited after the flag rollout stabilizes. ❌ The new AuthBroker path inherits three silent failure modes on day one, and auth is the wrong place to carry that debt.

answers.D7 \u2014 Issue 3 [P1] (confidence 9/10): 3A) Split per stage, one typed error boundary, fail closed (recommended)

questions.question:
D8 — Issue 4 [P1] (confidence 9/10) PLAN.md:14-16: how deep does coverage go for the new components?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Test section.
ELI10: The plan promises unit and integration coverage for "success/error paths" of the new components, which is a happy-path-plus-one-error promise. The diagram above shows 24 gaps. The ones that matter most are not the obvious ones: the suspend-during-mint race from 1A, the flag switch from 2A, and the one-of-five IDP calls failing. Those are the paths that only break in production, and they are exactly the ones "success/error paths" tends to skip. The legacyAuthFlow() and validateAndDispatch() characterization tests are already required by the regression rule and are not part of this question.
Stakes if we pick wrong: The two remedies you just approved (epoch drop, per-tenant flag) ship with no proof they work, and the first evidence is a suspended tenant still logged in.
Recommendation: 4A because with CC the full set costs about the same as the shortcut in wall-clock, and you said too many tests beats too few.
Completeness: 4A=10/10, 4B=7/10, 4C=4/10
Net: every branch in the diagram gets a test now vs. finding the untested branches in an incident.

options.label: 4A) Every diagram branch + contract + race + E2E (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Unit tests for every branch above; contract tests running AuthBroker against the real adapter (not a mock) for hit/miss/invalidate/epoch; a deterministic race test that suspends between mint start and write and asserts no entry lands; three E2E flows (canary login, suspended, revoked) per flag state (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min). ✅ Both approved remedies are proven before the flag ever flips. ❌ Largest test diff; the race test needs an injectable clock or hook to be deterministic.

options.label: 4B) Unit for all branches + E2E happy path
options.description: ✅ Every code branch in the diagram gets a unit test; one E2E login per flag state (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~25 min). ✅ Fast to run, no real-adapter wiring in tests. ❌ Adapter is mocked, so the epoch drop and hook wiring are never exercised together; suspended/revoked E2E flows are not covered.

options.label: 4C) Unit success + one error path per component
options.description: ✅ Matches the plan as written; smallest test diff (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min). ✅ Enough to catch compile-level and obvious logic mistakes. ❌ Race, flag switch, and partial IDP failure remain untested; the paths most likely to page you have no proof.

answers.D8 \u2014 Issue 4 [P1] (confidence 9/10): 4A) Every diagram branch + contract + race + E2E (recommended)

questions.question:
D9 — Issue 5 [P2] (confidence 7/10) PLAN.md:31-32: parallelize the 5 IDP calls, but with which failure rule, and are all 5 needed?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Performance section.
ELI10: Five sequential network calls to the identity provider on every token validation means login latency is five round trips added together. Promise.all makes that one round trip, and the plan is right that the calls are independent. But Promise.all also changes failure behavior: it rejects on the first failure and abandons the rest, which is exactly what you want in auth (fail closed, fast). The trap is that some engineers reach for Promise.allSettled to "handle partial failure," which in auth means deciding a token is valid when one check never ran. Second question the plan skips: in most IDP integrations, two of those five calls fetch data that changes rarely (discovery document, signing keys). Those belong in the existing cache adapter, which drops the per-request count to three or fewer.
Stakes if we pick wrong: allSettled with a lenient merge silently accepts tokens when the IDP is flaky; five parallel calls per request also multiplies IDP load five-fold at peak and can hit their rate limits.
Recommendation: 5A because Promise.all with a per-call timeout is the fail-closed, explicit choice, and caching the static IDP metadata reuses the adapter you already have. Maps to explicit-over-clever and to reuse before building.
Completeness: 5A=10/10, 5B=7/10, 5C=5/10
Net: fewer, faster, fail-closed calls vs. five parallel calls with undefined partial-failure behavior.

options.label: 5A) Promise.all + per-call timeout + cache static IDP metadata (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Promise.all over the per-request calls with an AbortController timeout on each; any rejection or timeout fails validation closed with the failing call named in the error (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min). ✅ Discovery document and JWKS cached through the existing adapter with TTL from the IDP's cache headers; per-request IDP calls drop to 3 or fewer and cold-start still works. ❌ Adds a key-rotation edge: a JWKS miss on an unknown kid must trigger one refetch before rejecting, which is one more branch to test.

options.label: 5B) Promise.all + per-call timeout, no metadata caching
options.description: ✅ Latency drops from 5 round trips to 1 with the fail-closed rule made explicit (human: ~2 h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ No new cache keys or TTL handling. ❌ Still 5 IDP calls per request at peak; rate limits and IDP outages hit 5x harder than necessary.

options.label: 5C) Plain Promise.all as the plan states
options.description: ✅ One-line change, exactly what PLAN.md:32 describes (human: ~15 min / CC: ~2 min). ✅ Latency win is captured. ❌ No timeout means one hung IDP call hangs the login indefinitely; failure semantics are left implicit for the next engineer to guess.

answers.D9 \u2014 Issue 5 [P2] (confidence 7/10): 5A) Promise.all + per-call timeout + cache static IDP metadata (recommended)

questions.question:
D10 — TODO 1: delete legacyAuthFlow() and the per-tenant flag after rollout completes.
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, TODOS.md updates (no TODOS.md exists yet; it would be created).
ELI10: Decision 2A keeps the legacy login path alive behind a flag during rollout. That is deliberate, but it leaves two login implementations in the codebase. Once every tenant is on AuthBroker and the flag has been at 100% for an agreed soak period, the legacy function, the routing switch, and the characterization tests that pin legacy behavior should all be removed in one small PR. Without a written TODO, dual paths tend to live forever.
What: Remove legacyAuthFlow(), the flag router, and legacy characterization tests. Why: two auth paths is permanent cognitive and security surface. Pros: smaller codebase, one path to audit. Cons: must wait for soak; deleting the oracle means the new path is now the only truth. Context: flag rollout per D6/2A; AuthBroker per D4. Depends on: 100% flag rollout + soak period (suggest 2 weeks) with zero legacy traffic.
Recommendation: A because the plan otherwise has no owner for the cleanup and it cannot be done in this PR by design.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: written follow-up vs. a dead code path nobody remembers to remove.

options.label: A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Cleanup has a written owner, trigger, and dependency; /ship and /retro will surface it (human: ~2 min / CC: ~1 min, write deferred until plan mode exits). ✅ Deletion PR later is trivial because the scope is recorded now. ❌ Creates TODOS.md in a repo that has none; one more file to keep current.

options.label: B) Skip — not valuable enough
options.description: ✅ No new file; team relies on memory or issue tracker. ✅ Zero effort now. ❌ Dual login paths have no recorded expiry; this is how legacy code becomes permanent.

options.label: C) Build it now in this PR
options.description: ✅ No follow-up needed; codebase ends with one path. ✅ Smallest final surface. ❌ Contradicts 2A: deleting legacy in the same PR removes the rollback path and the regression oracle.

questions.question:
D11 — TODO 2: metrics and alerts for stale-epoch drops and fail-closed IDP rejections.
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, TODOS.md updates.
ELI10: Decisions 1A and 5A both add a "drop and log" branch: a cache write with a stale epoch is discarded, and a failed or timed-out IDP call denies the login. Both are correct fail-closed behavior, and both are invisible unless someone reads logs. A counter per branch and an alert when the rate spikes tells you the difference between "one suspension raced a mint" and "the IDP is down and every tenant is locked out." This is observability, not core behavior, so it can follow the main PR.
What: emit counters for stale-epoch drops and IDP fail-closed rejections, tagged by tenant and cause; alert on rate. Why: fail-closed without visibility looks like random login failures to users and support. Pros: 3am triage becomes a dashboard glance. Cons: depends on whatever metrics stack exists, which the plan does not describe. Context: branches introduced by 1A and 5A. Depends on: main refactor PR landing; knowing the metrics library in use.
Recommendation: A because the fail-closed branches were just approved and shipping them blind is the one gap left; adding it now (C) is also defensible if the metrics library is already wired.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: know when fail-closed fires vs. learn about it from support tickets.

options.label: A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Captured with cause, tags, and dependency so it lands right after the main PR (human: ~2 min / CC: ~1 min, write deferred until plan mode exits). ✅ Keeps this PR focused on behavior and tests. ❌ Fail-closed branches ship without a counter for the gap between PRs.

options.label: B) Skip — not valuable enough
options.description: ✅ Structured logs from 3A already carry stage and tenant; grep works. ✅ Zero effort. ❌ No alert means an IDP outage locking out every tenant is discovered by users first.

options.label: C) Build it now in this PR
options.description: ✅ Counters land with the branches that need them; no gap (human: ~2 h / CC: ~10 min). ✅ Tests for the branches can assert the counter increments. ❌ Widens this PR into the metrics stack, which the plan has not described; adds a dependency to discover during implementation.
